The frozen backbone the adapter rides on:

## What it is

[Laya](https://laya.convaiinnovations.com/) is a 421M-parameter
non-autoregressive decision model: a from-scratch decision head on a frozen
ModernBERT-large bidirectional encoder. One state plus a map of typed
questions goes in, typed answers with probabilities come out, and it
generates no text.

It is a genuine member of this category, and it targets our contract
deliberately rather than by coincidence. Its inference entry point is
`system_one(state, questions)`, and the docstring in
[`rl_agent_api.py`](https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya/raw/main/rl_agent_api.py)
reads:

```python
"""Jev-compatible inference for a saved RL Agent model: system_one(state, questions) -> typed answers."""
```

Same three primitives under the same names — `choice`, `score`, `noul` — and
a confidence computed as `1 - normalized_entropy` under the comment
`"""Jev-style confidence"""`. Three checkpoints ship under Apache-2.0 with
downloadable weights, plus a router that picks between them from Unicode
script detection before the forward pass.

So: the closest open analogue to Kev that exists, and the largest of roughly
a dozen open reproductions that appeared in the same week — see
[awesome-jev](https://github.com/yibie/awesome-jev), which also lists a
`kev` on Qwen2.5-0.5B, `jev-local`, `LitJev`, and several

## Laya: learn from it, don't benchmark against it yet

## The band, before and after

A band is useful when items in a low band are wrong more often than items in
a high band. That is a stricter test than "the field varies", because a field
that varies at random also varies.

**Base model:**

| Band | Items | Correct | Accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `almost certainly not` | 16 | 15 | 0.94 |
| `unlikely` | 3 | 3 | 1.00 |
| `likely` | 77 | 61 | 0.79 |
| `almost certain` | 2 | 2 | 1.00 |

**Band adapter:**

| Band | Items | Correct | Accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `unlikely` | 14 | 9 | **0.64** |
| `likely` | 45 | 37 | **0.82** |
| `almost certain` | 39 | 37 | **0.95** |

The base model's band is not weak, it is **anti-informative**. Its lowest
band scores 0.94 and its second-lowest scores 1.00, while the bulk of items —
77 of 98 — pile into `likely` at 0.79. Reading it would mislead you.

The adapter's band is monotone across all three bands it uses, with real
spread: 0.64, 0.82, 0.95. **That is a usable certainty signal, and it is the
first one Lev has had.** Trained on 98 records in about four minutes.

## The read counter is stricter than I asked for

`Suite::partition` **refuses** `Locked` outright. The only path is a `LockedLedger` — append-only JSONL, meant to be committed — and a second read against the same digest is refused by default, naming the earlier read's date and subject. Taking one anyway requires an explicit override that records the authority and the argument.

It went deliberately stricter than kev upstream, which allows one read per published candidate. Its reasoning: per-candidate keying permits exactly the failure this issue exists to prevent — six candidates, six reads. That's the right call and it's documented in the module. ## What's now enforced

`verify_chain` distinguishes the two kinds of dishonesty as *values*, not prose — `ChainFault::Edited` versus `ChainFault::Resequenced` — so callers branch without string-matching. The messages name the row and say which it was: contents digesting differently means the row was edited after it was written; a predecessor mismatch means rows were inserted, removed, or reordered.

Single-writer is enforced with an exclusive lock file that holds **across processes**, not just threads.

## Three things it added that I didn't ask for, all correct

**The byte assertion caught a second failure mode.** The test compares `fs::read` before and after a refused append *and* asserts no lock file was left behind — a refusal that stranded the lock would wedge the store as surely as one that wrote.

**A store whose last line lacks a trailing newline is refused before appending**, because the new row would otherwise be joined onto the truncated one. That's a real corruption path I hadn't considered.

**`append_sealed` refuses a row whose receipt doesn't match its own contents**, so a tampered row can't be admitted even when it names the right predecessor.

## One thing my issue got wrong

I specified the store as row-agnostic, and it can't quite be: the duplicate rule and the schema allowlist both need field names. So `store::EVAL_ROW_SCHEMA` currently duplicates `row::SCHEMA` as a string literal.

## It derived the Brier bound I said to derive, then showed the derivation can't be the threshold

For a bin of width `w`, replacing raw `p` with bin accuracy `a` costs at most `2·w·accuracy`. On a 30-item family that's two bins, `w = 0.5`, ceiling **≈ 0.73 absolute** against a raw Brier of 0.173 — an order of magnitude looser than any usable tolerance.

So the honest conclusion is: **the derivation catches a bug, not a bad table.** The tenth stays a *labelled judgment*, with the case that tuned it recorded in the bound's own `why` field, inside the digest. That's a better answer than either of the two I offered in the issue, and it's the kind of thing I'd have been tempted to paper over.

## It refused to invent the one threshold it couldn't measure

An absolute minimum accuracy gain can't be chosen honestly until #9370 measures the suite's resampling variance — the seeds are `0..n` and reproduce exactly, so there's no spread to derive from. Instead of picking a number it recorded `variance_basis: "item_sampling"` and a `pending_measurement` naming #9370, **both inside the digest**, so filling it produces `decision-v2` by construction. Every gain verdict carries "the standard error covers item sampling only" in its own detail line.

The decision effect size isn't a constant at all — it's two standard errors of the measured accuracies, computed per comparison, so a thin split raises its own bar. On my adapter result the bound is 0.104 and the win is 0.130: **it clears by under three points.**

- The choice adapter: **`passed` on decision, `failed` on probability**, with the two confident-wrongness criteria as the failures and +13 accuracy unable to rescue them.

you can make any open source model behave like jev with just a bit of inference engineering.  

it's shockingly easy. to prove it, we built a new endpoint we're calling deepseek-v4.1-flash-jev. see the demo below. here's how it's done:

sglang (an inference engine) offers a scoring endpoint in addition to the normal generation one. in scoring mode, given an input & set of possible answers, it forces the model to produce probabilities for each one. example:

> input: what is most common letter in abcccde?
> possible answers: a, b, c
> output: (c, 0.9), (b, 0.0.5), (a, 0.05)

getting the above behavior instead of streamed output is as simple as using sglang's /v1/score endpoint instead of /generate. there's just one other trick required.

for deepseek, you have to add a closing think tag before the response. this forces a direct answer instead of  a reasoning trace. if you want reasoning, you can do that too, but imo that makes things too slow to be worth it.

dsv4.1 flash is not as good as jev, but if we had enough spare compute to experiment with this same approach for a larger model then i think the decision quality would be at least as good, if not better.

transcript.text:
Third research doc pushed. This one I could ground in data we already had.

## We've already run a version of this experiment

The claim is that fine-tuning beats hosted Jev on the task. **Kev is the evidence, from the other side.** It's 0.5B, Banking77 was in its training mix at 1,500 records, and its card reports:

| | Banking77 |
|---|---|
| kev-0.5b, held-out split | **0.860** |
| hosted Jev, published | 0.870 |

A half-billion-parameter specialist roughly matches the hosted generalist on a task it was trained for. The direction of the claim is right and we didn't need GLiNER to learn it.

**And the same card says what it costs, in the same table it reports the win:** in-distribution only, BoolQ and MNLI far below state of the art, and the preview family trailing Jev by **8 to 26 points out of domain**. The specialist wins on its task and loses everywhere else by a margin large enough that the trade *is* the decision.

Laya is a third point on the same benchmark failing a different way — 0.425, a context ceiling rather than a capability gap. Banking77 punishes a small context as hard as it rewards fine-tuning.

## Three things the claim doesn't address

**Is GLiNER a decision model at all?** Its lineage is span-based entity recognition, which makes it a strong *classifier* — one of three primitives. A Noul is a probability that a statement holds; a Score is a weighted position on an *ordered* rubric. If it does neither, "beats Jev" is a claim about a third of the contract.

**Calibration isn't mentioned.** Accuracy is the easy half. A margin passed through a sigmoid isn't a probability about the world, and it's the calibration that lets code route on a threshold rather than just take the argmax.

**Do options interact?** Hosted Jev demonstrably lets them. A model scoring each label independently and normalizing afterwards can't — which matters for "none of the above" and anything listwise.

Also worth saying: it's a self-run fine-tune against a *quoted* hosted figure. **Ours has exactly the same shape a
A/B landed, and it exposes a gap that blocks my biggest claimed win. Filing that now.

#9370 measured the seed-block spread for **accuracy** (σ = 0.0197) and mean top share. It did not measure ECE, Brier, or log loss.

#9372 built the A/B on that measurement and correctly refused to invent floors for the three it lacks. It records them in \`Rule::pending_measurements\` inside the gate digest, and the consequence is stated plainly there: **a win on ECE, Brier, or log loss is \`unverifiable\` and can never earn a keep.**

## Why that is urgent rather than tidy

The largest result claimed this week is a calibration result. Conditioning the map on a trained certainty band cut log loss from **2.601 to 0.388** where a pooled map did not help at all — that is the finding that moved Lev's overconfidence, and it is the reason the band adapter was worth training.

Under the gate as it now stands, that result **cannot be confirmed**. Not refused — unverifiable. There is no floor to compare it against, and a 85% reduction is treated the same as a 1% one.

Four things I'd push back on, one of them hard.

## It collapses "decision" into "classification"

Every leaf picks a label. But the contract has three primitives, and only one of them is classification. BERT and EmbeddingGemma do Choice. They don't do a **Noul** — a probability that a statement holds — and they don't do a **Score**, a weighted position on an *ordered* rubric where the ordering has to mean something.

Every leaf is justified on cost, flexibility, or capability. None on whether the number it returns means anything. That's the axis that decides whether your code can route on a threshold or can only take the argmax — and a BERT softmax is not calibrated by default any more than anything else is.

We spent today learning this expensively: conditioning on a trained certainty band cut log loss 2.601 → 0.388, where a pooled map didn't help at all. Nothing in the tree would tell you that problem exists.

The tree implies Jev is the no-labels option. It is — for *getting started*. But the moment you care whether it's right, **you need labelled outcomes anyway**, and once you have them the fine-tune branch opens.

## The structural finding

**GLiNER 2.5 cannot serve Score.** `ordinal()` reports the *argmax's index* — with levels calm/frustrated/very-frustrated it returns 0, 1, or 2 and never 1.4. There's no expected-value computation anywhere in the repo.

And you can't just compute `Σ i·p_i` yourself: the loss is **independent per-label BCE** and **candidate order is shuffled every training step**. Nothing teaches the model that one level is further along an axis than another. So the ordering carries no metric.

That shuffling also settles the option-interaction question — and not the way either side assumed. Options *do* co-encode; the repo's own source warns that narrowing the task set is *"a different measurement, not a filter."* But the interaction is an incidental encoder artifact the training objective actively pushes against.

The socket is the same shape and **won't take weights**. ## Jev, Kev, and Lev, one client, live

I ran all three behind the same `POST /v1/systemone` contract — the real `crates/jev` client, nothing changed but `base_url`:

| Door | Correct | Mean confidence | Confident errors | Latency |
|---|---|---|---|---|

| kev (`kev-serve`, local) | 1 of 8 | 0.81 | 4 | 182 ms |

Eight items doesn't rank models. What it proves is that the contract holds across three implementations.

**Kev's 1 of 8 is a real bug, not a quality gap.** It answers `other` on every item except the one whose answer is `other` — a constant argmax, the signature of a readout that isn't reading. `kev-0.5b`'s own card reports 0.94 on a four-option classification. I posted the repro on **#9342** (its conformance issue) and did not touch `crates/kev`.

## The finding that changed the design

Issue #9346 was written with a stop condition, and the measurement hit it. **Sampling spread does not track difficulty** — top share runs 0.81 to 1.00 across easy and hard items alike, and both wrong answers sit at 0.81 as steadily as the right ones. The certainty band came back `likely` on all eight items, including both wrong ones.

So there is no signal to calibrate. I changed a rule rather than pretend otherwise: the door serves the sampling frequency, marks it `uncalibrated` in every response and in `/v1/models`, and returns a typed 409 when a caller sends `require_calibration`. Reproducibility came out better than assumed — greedy is deterministic and a seed reproduces its sample 16/16 in-process and across processes.

**Why:** everything around training a Lev adapter is built and tested —

   confirm it any time by running
   `python3 training/lev-adapter/toolkit.py` in `~/work/openagents`, which
   prints the prefix the device reports.
4. Unpack it to `~/work/openagents/training/lev-adapter/toolkit/`, or put it
   anywhere and set `LEV_TOOLKIT_ROOT` to that path. The directory is
   gitignored — do not commit it, since its terms do not permit
   redistribution and the repository is public.
5. Tell the agent, or run the five steps in
   `~/work/openagents/training/lev-adapter/README.md`.

issue for the training run itself.

**Note:** if an OS update changes the on-device base model, the prefix in
step 3 changes with it, and any adapter trained against the old base stops
loading. `lev-serve` refuses to start on a mismatch rather than serving a bad
pairing.

On that page (you're signed in now), the left sidebar has **Overview / What's New / Get Started / Resources**. The download lives in the **Toolkit** section of the main content — a version table with three rows. The two betas are withdrawn; take **26.0.0**. Clicking its download makes you accept the toolkit terms first, then the file comes down.

The download links only render for signed-in Developer Program members, which is why I couldn't see or fetch them.

Then:

```
unzip ~/Downloads/adapter_training_toolkit_v26_0_0*.zip -d ~/work/openagents/training/lev-adapter/
```

Then tell me and I'll run the training.

## Two things I had wrong, now fixed

Reading Apple's documented commands, my drivers had real bugs that would have cost you a failed run:

- **`train.py` invented `--rank` and `--seed`.** The toolkit's CLI doesn't have them — it takes `--epochs`, `--learning-rate`, `--batch-size`. Removed, and `--batch-size 4` added.
- **`export.py` passed the checkpoint *directory*.** Apple's exporter wants the file, `adapter-final.pt`. That fails late and confusingly. Fixed, with a clear error if it's missing, plus optional `--draft-checkpoint`.

One default I'm deliberately keeping against Apple's docs: they suggest learning rate `1e-3`; I default to `1e-4`. Kev's research log found the single largest quality effect it measured was that too high a rate erodes the base knowledge the task depends on. It's a flag, so easy to override if the first run underfits.

## #259 is done — both halves landed, issue closed

**Server** (`c303a37`): allowance moved off the config constant onto `users.credit_allowance_microusd`. `account_credit_microusd` is now `20_000_000` and is the *default a new row gets*; the column is what `Credit.allowance/1` reads. **CLI** (`7cbe78af4f`): the balance renders on the bottom row, refreshed at session open and after every settled turn.

### The deletion hole was real, and worse than I guessed

I filed that issue guessing delete-and-resignup would mint a fresh row. Wrong mechanism. `DataRights.delete/3` **deliberately retains the user row** (so deletion can't erase a ban), so the unique index holds and you get the same row back.

But `inference_grants.owner_visitor_id` cascades off `visitors`, and deletion drops the visitor root — so `spent/1` reads **zero** again and the account recovers its **entire balance. Once per deletion. Indefinitely.** An unlimited credit farm through the data-rights endpoint, which is a path nobody would think to audit for billing.

Fix: the allowance absorbs the erased spend before the row goes, so `allowance − spent` is identical either side of a deletion. The mutable side is the allowance — which is where a top-up would land anyway.

### It also refused to print a caveated dollar figure

Four states, and **two carry no number at all**: `credit: unavailable` (a read that didn't answer, replacing any stale figure), `credit: 3 unpriced calls`, and `$18.40 left` only when the server calls its spend complete. Its reasoning beats the `≤ $18.40` I'd suggested — *a caveated number loses to the number when the number never moves.* Readers take the digits and drop the qualifier.

The #118 agent caught something in itself that nobody had flagged: it had reported a clean `/tmp` credential sweep, but **the sweep had been killed, not completed** — it read a log showing a header with nothing under it and treated that as "no hits."

That's a fourth distinct thread, and the one most likely to recur:

|---|---|
| 1 | A value that looks more certain than it is — unknown cost, stale identity |
| 2 | A waiver deletes the signal that catches your own worst failure |
| 3 | A test's meaning isn't preserved by a clean merge; green isn't evidence |

# GLM-5.3-Flash

<Tip>
  GLM-5.3-Flash is now fully available on the [GLM Coding Plan](https://z.ai/subscribe). With native multimodal capabilities and 3× the quota, it delivers a smoother and more cost-effective coding experience.

## Model Overview

GLM-5.3-Flash is the first native multimodal model in the GLM-5 series, delivering stronger intelligence than GLM-5.2 while maintaining an exceptionally cost-efficient architecture.

* **Highly Efficient Hybrid Architecture**

GLM-5.3-Flash has 320B total parameters, with 18B activated parameters. It is the first open-source frontier model to adopt a hybrid architecture combining sparse attention and linear attention. This architecture significantly reduces computational and serving costs while maintaining precise long-context capabilities. Compared with GLM-5.3, it reduces attention computation and KV cache size by 3.01× and 4.44×, respectively.

* **Native Multimodal Visual Coding**

Visual capabilities are natively integrated into the coding loop, enabling the model to actively observe interfaces, rendered results, and interaction feedback, and continuously test and improve its work accordingly. From frontend development and game creation to Blender 3D scenes and real-world environment operation driven by BUA and CUA, the model can seamlessly coordinate tasks across code, browsers, and graphical user interfaces.

* **A Professional Work Partner Beyond Coding**

GLM-5.3-Flash further extends its capabilities to a wide range of professional workflows, including Office tasks, financial research, and professional document processing. It can autonomously break down complex objectives, invoke the appropriate tools, and review and optimize its outputs, completing end-to-end workflows from research and analysis and model building to delivering finished PPTX, PDF, DOCX, and XLSX files.

[↗ blog](https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.3-flash)

#### **Model API**

**Model Code**：`glm-5.3-flash`\
**API Documentation**：[Chat Completion API](https://docs.z.ai/api-reference/introduction)\
**Parameter Settings**：Text parameters are consistent with GLM-5.3, with support for a 1M-token context window.\
**Image Parameters**：Add a content block with `type: image_url` to` messages[].content[]`, and pass the image URL (recommended) or a Base64 Data URL through `image_url.url`. Multiple images can be added by including multiple `image_url` content blocks.\
**Recommended Settings**： `temperature: 1`, `top_p: 0.95`, and `reasoning_effort: max`. `thinking.type` only supports `enabled`; we recommend setting `thinking.clear_thinking: false`. For streaming requests, we recommend enabling both stream: true and `tool_stream: true`.

#### **GLM Coding Plan**

Now fully available, GLM-5.3-Flash can be used with your preferred tools, with 3× the available quota compared with GLM-5.3.\
The new GLM Coding Plan adopts a points-based quota system with transparent usage limits. Model calls made during off-peak hours, including all day on weekends, consume only 50% of the standard points.\
